```{python}
ex = mf.example()
st = mf.spatial_story()
kp, beta = ex["kp"], ex["beta"]
df, gam = mf.load_or_run(R=30)
dc = df[df.scenario == "correct"]
s = mf.summary(dc).set_index(["stage", "fit"])
ss = mf.summary(dc, by=("season",))
sc = mf.summary(df, by=("scenario",))
DR, KR = mf.STAGE_LAB["dr"], mf.STAGE_LAB["krige"]
b = lambda st, f: s.loc[(st, mf.FIT_LAB[f]), "bias"]
bs = lambda scen, st, f, col="bias": sc.set_index(["scenario", "stage", "fit"]).loc[(scen, st, mf.FIT_LAB[f]), col]
prof = ex["prof"]
rms_mu = {f: np.sqrt(np.mean([((mf.mean_at(beta, f, sx.GX, sx.GY, ex["times"][k], mf.grid_lq(ex, k))
                                - mf.mean_true(sx.GX, sx.GY, ex["times"][k]))**2).mean()
                               for k in range(0, mf.N_SNAP, mf.TARGET_EVERY)])) for f in mf.FITS}
n_win = np.array([((np.abs(mf._wrap(prof.x.values - cx)) <= mf.LAM_W) & (np.abs(prof.y.values - cy) <= mf.LAM_W)).sum()
                  for cx, cy in mf.CENTERS])
eta_prof = (prof.z - mf.mean_true(prof.x, prof.y, prof.t)).mean()
```

Kriging predicts a field as a mean field plus a GP anomaly. Where floats are sparse the anomaly
reverts to zero and the map falls back on the mean field, so a mean field fitted to preferentially
sampled profiles carries their bias into the gaps. This report compares four fits of the mean
field on the toy jet of [the toy report](simex.qmd), two global and two local in the style of
Roemmich--Gilson and Kuusela--Stein, each followed by the same kriging step.

## Toy with a meander and a seasonal cycle

The field is the Bickley-jet OHC with a standing meander, plus a seasonal cycle whose amplitude
varies with both latitude and longitude:
$$
Z(x,y,t) = \underbrace{-\tanh(y/L) + m\,\operatorname{sech}^2(y/L)\cos(k_m x) + a(x,y)\cos\!\big(2\pi(t-t_0)/365\big)}_{\mu(x,y,t)} \;+\; \eta(x,y,t),
$$
$$
a(x,y) = 0.3\,\big\{1+\tfrac12\tanh(y/L)\big\}\big\{1+\tfrac12\sin(2\pi x/L_x)\big\},
$$
with $m = `{python} f"{mf.MEANDER}"`$, $k_m = 4\pi/L_x$ (wavelength
$`{python} f"{2 * np.pi / mf.K_M:.0f}"`$ km), and $\eta$ the travelling-eddy part of the jet
streamfunction. The meander is a stationary mode of the streamfunction, so the floats and the
clouds both follow it. The seasonal term is thermal only. $\eta$ and the meander integrate to zero
over the periodic channel, so the box mean is
$\bar Z(t) = \int Z(\cdot,t)\,d\mathbb P = 0.3\cos\{2\pi(t-t_0)/365\}$ exactly.

Sixty floats are deployed uniformly on day $0$. After a one-year spin-up, $4$ years of $10$-day
profiles give $146$ snapshots and $8{,}760$ profiles per replicate. In the example replicate below,
`{python} f"{(prof.y < 0).mean():.0%}"` of profiles are in the warm southern half, and within a
latitude band they also favour warm eddies: the anomaly $\eta$ averages
`{python} f"{eta_prof:+.3f}"` at the profiles against $0$ over the box.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Z in the warm and cold seasons with that snapshot's floats, and the box mean through the record."
_show_fig(mf.plot_setup(ex))
```

## Four mean fits

**Global fits.** One regression over the whole box on the basis $h(y,t)$: a cubic in
$u = y/250$ km, the annual harmonics, and the harmonics times $u$. The basis has no $x$ terms, so
it cannot represent the meander or the zonal change in seasonal amplitude; it stands in for a mean
field fitted on too coarse a scale. $\log\hat q_t(x,y)$ is the stacked cloud density from anchors
$4$ cycles back (as in the toy report), relative to uniform and floored at $0.05$.

**Local fits.** Following Ridgway et al. (2002), Roemmich and Gilson (2009) and Kuusela and Stein
(2018), for each centre $s^* = (x^*,y^*)$ of a $`{python} f"{mf.CX_N}"` \times `{python} f"{mf.CY_N}"`$
grid ($\approx 25$ km spacing), the window
$\mathcal W(s^*) = [x^*-\lambda, x^*+\lambda]\times[y^*-\lambda,y^*+\lambda]$ with
$\lambda = `{python} f"{mf.LAM_W:.0f}"`$ km (periodic in $x$) is formed, and the profiles in it are
fitted by least squares to
$$
m_{s^*}(x,y,t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\Delta_x + \beta_2\Delta_y + \beta_3\Delta_x\Delta_y + \beta_4\Delta_x^2 + \beta_5\Delta_y^2
+ \sum_{k=1}^{6}\big\{\gamma_k\sin(2\pi k t/365) + \delta_k\cos(2\pi k t/365)\big\} + \nu_1(t-t_D) + \nu_2(t-t_D)^2,
$$
with $(\Delta_x,\Delta_y) = (x-x^*, y-y^*)$ and $t_D$ the middle of the record. The window mean is
$\hat\mu(s^*,t) = \hat m_{s^*}(s^*,t)$, the intercept, harmonics and trend. Off the centres,
$\hat\mu(\cdot,t)$ is the bilinear interpolant of the centre coefficients; this interpolation is our
choice, not part of the RG/KS specification. A window with fewer than $`{python} f"{mf.N_MIN}"`$
profiles would be widened by $25\%$ steps. In the example replicate every window already has at
least `{python} f"{n_win.min()}"` profiles (median `{python} f"{np.median(n_win):.0f}"`). The
local $+\log\hat q$ fit adds $\gamma\log\hat q_t(x,y)$ to $m_{s^*}$ and keeps
$\hat\gamma_{s^*}\log\hat q_t$ in $\hat\mu$, so its $\hat q$ coefficient varies by window.

| fit | coefficients | intuition |
|---|---|---|
| global OLS | $\hat\beta = (H^\top H)^{-1}H^\top z$ | every profile is one vote, one mean shape for the box |
| global GLS + $\log\hat q$ | $\hat\beta = (H^\top K^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top K^{-1}z$, $\log\hat q$ a column of $H$ | correlated profiles share a vote; crowded water may be warmer |
| local LS (RG/KS) | ordinary least squares in each window | each place gets its own mean and seasonal cycle |
| local LS + $\log\hat q$ | as local LS, with $\log\hat q$ a column in each window | as above, and crowding may be warmer, by a different amount in each window |

$K$ is the anomaly covariance at the profiles: block diagonal by year (years as i.i.d. replicates),
anisotropic exponential in $(x,y,t)$ with a $10^{-3}$ relative nugget. Its parameters are *oracle*
values, the $e$-folding scales of the true $\eta$
($\ell_x = `{python} f"{kp['lx']:.0f}"`$ km, $\ell_y = `{python} f"{kp['ly']:.0f}"`$ km,
$\ell_t = `{python} f"{kp['lt']:.0f}"`$ d), so that only the mean-field step differs between fits.
The local fits are ordinary least squares, as in RG/KS; $K$ enters them only through kriging.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Example replicate. Left: zonal mean of each fitted mean field against the zonal mean of the true mean field on one cold-season day (the zonal mean hides the meander). Middle: latitude distribution of all profiles (dashed: uniform). Right: box mean of each fitted mean field alone, against the truth."
_show_fig(mf.plot_fits(ex))
```

Global OLS lets the crowded south and its warm eddies dominate, so its mean field runs warm. The
local fit follows the meander and the zonal change in the seasonal amplitude, which lowers the root-mean-square error of the mean
field over the box and the target days in this replicate from `{python} f"{rms_mu['ols']:.3f}"` to
`{python} f"{rms_mu['loc']:.3f}"`. Its box mean is
nevertheless almost as warm as the global OLS mean (right panel). Least squares within a window is
still one vote per profile, so each window is pulled toward the warm water its floats crowd into.

The $\log\hat q$ column lets a fit attribute the extra warmth of crowded water to the crowding
itself. Globally, $\hat\gamma = `{python} f"{beta['glsq'][-1]:.2f}"`$ here, and it also shifts the
latitude coefficients, because $\hat q$ itself varies with latitude. $\hat\gamma$ is therefore part
of a better prediction, not an interpretable effect. Within a $300$ km window $\log\hat q$ varies
less and is close to collinear with the quadratic terms. The window coefficients
$\hat\gamma_{s^*}$ are then noisy, and the local $+\log\hat q$ mean field is rougher than the
local one (root-mean-square error `{python} f"{rms_mu['locq']:.3f}"`) but less biased in its box
mean.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Left: expected float density q-hat on one day. Right: the true anomaly eta, with the contour where q-hat is twice uniform. Floats are expected where eta is warm."
_show_fig(mf.plot_q_term(ex))
```


## Three estimators of the box mean

**Kriging.** Each fitted mean field is followed by simple kriging of the residuals,
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{K}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \hat\mu(\cdot,t^*)\,d\mathbb P \;+\; \sum_i w_i\,\big\{Z_i - \hat\mu(x_i)\big\},
$$
with block-kriging weights $w_i$ from all profiles within $\pm 30$ d of $t^*$. The weights depend
only on the profile positions and $K$, so they are the same for the four fits; only the residuals
differ.

**Cross-fit DR, leave one float out.** For each float $f$, the map $\hat m^{(-f)}$ is the mean
fit plus kriging computed without any of float $f$'s profiles; for the local fits every window is
refit. In the two $\log\hat q$ fits, the covariate comes from the other floats' clouds only. The pooled $\hat q$ at a time after $t^*$ is
anchored partly on float $f$'s own positions near $t^*$, so using it would let float $f$'s realized
position into the map that float $f$ checks. With $q_f$ the cloud density of float $f$ (expected
profiles per km$^2$), $q = \sum_f q_f$ the stacked density, and $|\mathcal X|$ the box area,
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \sum_{f}\frac{q_f}{q}\,\hat m^{(-f)}\,d\mathbb P
\;+\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal X|}\sum_{f}\sum_{i\in f}\frac{Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)}{q(x_i)}\,\mathbf 1_{C}(x_i),
$$
where $C = \{q\,|\mathcal X|/n \ge 0.05\}$ is the covered set. Off $C$ the $n$ maps are averaged
with equal weight and no correction is made. The map term is not the full-data map. Each float's
own influence on the map is removed in proportion to where that float was expected to be, which is
what keeps a float from checking a map it helped build. Floats move independently given the flow.
Conditional on the other floats, Campbell's theorem gives
$\mathbb E\sum_{i\in f} g(x_i) = \int g\,q_f\,d\mu$, so if the clouds' density were exact,
$$
\mathbb E\big[\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*)\big] - \bar Z(t^*) \;=\; -\int_{C^c}\Big(Z - \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_f \mathbb E\,\hat m^{(-f)}\Big)\,d\mathbb P .
$$
This is an exact identity, with a positivity remainder on the uncovered set only. With estimated
densities $\hat q_f$ the bias picks up the product term
$\sum_f\int (Z-\hat m^{(-f)})(q_f-\hat q_f)/\hat q\,d\mathbb P$. Under the correct cloud model, that
error comes only from Monte Carlo and kernel smoothing in $\hat q_f$ ($200$ particles per cloud,
$10$ km bandwidth) and from binning to the $5$ km grid. On average $C$ covers
`{python} f"{dc.cover.mean():.1%}"` of the box.

The DR step is applied to all four mean fits. Estimates are taken at every third snapshot of each
of `{python} df.rep.nunique()` replicates. The $60$ leave-one-out kriging maps share one
cross-covariance per target. Each needs only the solve
$K_{-f}^{-1}\,(Z-\hat\mu^{(-f)})$, so leave-one-float-out costs little more than a single map.

## One day, map by map

The figures below follow the example replicate through one cold-season day (day
`{python} f"{st['t']:.0f}"`) under the correct cloud model. All maps share the colour scale of
$Z$, and all errors share one diverging scale. The box mean of each map is in its title. A single
day shows how each estimator builds its answer, not how well it does on average; that is the next
section.

**Mean field.** Each fit's $\hat\mu(\cdot, t^*)$ next to the true $\mu$. The global fits vary
only with latitude, as their basis allows, apart from the $\hat q$ pattern that the GLS
$+\log\hat q$ fit adds. The local fits follow the meander. The local $+\log\hat q$ fit adds its
window-by-window $\hat q$ term on top.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: the true mean field and the four fitted mean fields on one day. Bottom: their errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude."
_show_fig(mf.plot_mean_maps(st))
```

**Mean field + kriging.** Kriging adds the anomaly near the floats. Where floats are dense the
four maps agree and follow the eddies. In the gaps they fall back to their own mean field, so
the mean-field errors above survive there.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: the true field with that day's floats, and the kriging map built on each mean field. Bottom: map errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude."
_show_fig(mf.plot_krige_maps(st))
```

**Cross-fit DR.** Top row: the map term, the mixture
$\sum_f (q_f/q)\,\hat m^{(-f)}$ of the $60$ leave-one-float-out maps. Each float's own map is used
where that float was expected to be, so the mixture is close to the kriging map but never lets a
float check itself. Bottom row: each float's check $Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)$, coloured by the
residual and sized by its weight $1/q$, over the faint error of the mixed map. Isolated floats
far from the crowd get the largest weights: the northern floats are
`{python} f"{(st['xy'][:, 1] > 0).mean():.0%}"` of the floats on this day but carry
`{python} f"{st['weight'][st['xy'][:, 1] > 0].sum() / st['weight'].sum():.0%}"` of the weight. The weighted sum of the checks is the correction
added to the map term.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: weight of each float's check, and the mixed leave-one-out map for each mean fit. Bottom: map error by latitude, and each float's residual against its own leave-one-out map (size: weight)."
_show_fig(mf.plot_dr_maps(st))
```

## Results under the correct cloud model

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Error of the box-mean estimate over 30 replicates and about 49 target days each, correct cloud model."
_show_fig(mf.plot_errors(df))
```

```{python}
HTML(fmt(mf.summary(dc)))
```

`bias` and `sd` are the mean and standard deviation of the error over all replicate-days. `se` is
the Monte Carlo standard error of the bias, computed from the $30$ replicate-level mean errors, and
`bias_over_se` compares the two.

- **Mean field alone.** Global OLS and the local fit are biased by similar amounts
  (`{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'ols'):+.3f}"` and `{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'loc'):+.3f}"`),
  so fitting locally fixes the shape of the mean field but not its preferential-sampling bias.
  Adding $\log\hat q$ cuts the bias to `{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'glsq'):+.3f}"` (global GLS)
  and `{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'locq'):+.3f}"` (local). For comparison, the simple mean of a
  snapshot's profiles is biased by `{python} f"{s.loc[('simple mean of profiles', ''), 'bias']:+.3f}"`.
- **After kriging.** Kriging repairs the mean field where floats are dense. The biases become
  `{python} f"{b(KR, 'ols'):+.3f}"` (global OLS), `{python} f"{b(KR, 'loc'):+.3f}"` (local),
  `{python} f"{b(KR, 'glsq'):+.3f}"` (global GLS + $\log\hat q$) and
  `{python} f"{b(KR, 'locq'):+.4f}"` (local + $\log\hat q$). The last is within
  `{python} f"{abs(s.loc[(KR, mf.FIT_LAB['locq']), 'bias_over_se']):.0f}"` Monte Carlo standard error of
  zero; with the correct cloud model, the local fit with the $\hat q$ covariate leaves no bias that
  kriging cannot remove.
- **Cross-fit DR.** On the two maps without $\hat q$, DR is unbiased within Monte Carlo error:
  `{python} f"{b(DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"` (global OLS map) and `{python} f"{b(DR, 'loc'):+.4f}"` (local
  map). On the two $\log\hat q$ maps it is `{python} f"{b(DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"` and
  `{python} f"{b(DR, 'locq'):+.4f}"`, which are small but
  `{python} f"{s.loc[(DR, mf.FIT_LAB['glsq']), 'bias_over_se']:.0f}"` and
  `{python} f"{s.loc[(DR, mf.FIT_LAB['locq']), 'bias_over_se']:.0f}"` standard errors from zero. A
  likely cause, not yet tested, is that the covariate and the weights are built from the same
  cloud particles. The Monte Carlo error in $\hat q$ then enters both $\hat m^{(-f)}$ and $1/\hat q$,
  so the product term $\int (Z-\hat m)(q-\hat q)/\hat q\,d\mathbb P$ is no longer a product of
  independent errors. Building the covariate from independent particle draws would test this.
- **Variance.** The local map gives the least variable DR estimate
  (sd `{python} f"{s.loc[(DR, mf.FIT_LAB['loc']), 'sd']:.3f}"`, against
  `{python} f"{s.loc[(DR, mf.FIT_LAB['ols']), 'sd']:.3f}"` on the global OLS map), because its
  residuals are smaller. The local $+\log\hat q$ kriging map is still less variable than any DR
  estimate (sd `{python} f"{s.loc[(KR, mf.FIT_LAB['locq']), 'sd']:.3f}"`, RMSE
  `{python} f"{s.loc[(KR, mf.FIT_LAB['locq']), 'rmse']:.3f}"`), so under the correct cloud model it
  has the lowest per-day RMSE. The sd is per target day and averages down over many days, but a
  bias does not.

## Misspecified cloud models

The real floats always move in the true flow. The clouds, and so $\hat q$, are now drawn from four
wrong models, the same ones as in [the toy report](simex.qmd):

- the weak drift toward warm water is left out;
- the eddies are displaced by a quarter wavelength;
- the cloud noise is too small ($K/4$);
- the cloud noise is too large ($4K$).

The wrong $\hat q$ enters the $\log\hat q$ covariate, the mixing weights $q_f/q$, the residual
weights $1/q$, and the covered set. The global OLS and local maps do not use $\hat q$, so for them
only the DR correction changes.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Bias of the four DR estimators (filled) and of the local + log q-hat kriging map (open), under each cloud model. Bars: 95% Monte Carlo intervals."
_show_fig(mf.plot_scenarios(df))
```

```{python}
t = sc[(sc.stage == DR) | ((sc.stage == KR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB["locq"]))]
t = t.assign(scenario=t.scenario.map(mf.sx.SCEN_LAB))
HTML(fmt(t[["scenario", "stage", "fit", "bias", "se", "bias_over_se", "sd", "rmse"]]))
```

With a wrong cloud model, DR is no longer unbiased. Its bias is then the product term: the map's
residuals times the error in $\hat q$. The quality of the map starts to matter.

- **Drift omitted, or noise too large.** The clouds no longer concentrate where floats actually
  gather, so the weights are too flat and the correction is too small. The local $+\log\hat q$
  map gives the smallest DR bias in both cases (`{python} f"{bs('no_conv', DR, 'locq'):+.4f}"` and
  `{python} f"{bs('K_large', DR, 'locq'):+.4f}"`), at most half that of the other three maps
  (`{python} f"{bs('no_conv', DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"` and `{python} f"{bs('K_large', DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"`
  on the global OLS map).
- **Eddies displaced.** $\hat q$ is high in the wrong places, so the covariate carries little
  information (the global $\hat\gamma$ falls to
  `{python} f"{gam[gam.scenario == 'shifted'].gamma.mean():.3f}"`), and the four DR estimators end up
  similar (`{python} f"{sc[(sc.scenario == 'shifted') & (sc.stage == DR)].bias.min():+.4f}"` to
  `{python} f"{sc[(sc.scenario == 'shifted') & (sc.stage == DR)].bias.max():+.4f}"`). That is
  still below the kriging maps' bias.
- **Noise too small.** This is the dangerous direction. Clouds that are too tight give floats
  landing in their thin tails very large weights, so DR over-corrects. On the maps without
  $\hat q$ the bias becomes `{python} f"{bs('K_small', DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"` (global OLS) and
  `{python} f"{bs('K_small', DR, 'loc'):+.4f}"` (local), larger in size than the uncorrected
  kriging bias and of the opposite sign. On the $\log\hat q$ maps, whose residuals are small, it
  is `{python} f"{bs('K_small', DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"` (global) and
  `{python} f"{bs('K_small', DR, 'locq'):+.4f}"` (local). Coverage also drops to
  `{python} f"{df[df.scenario == 'K_small'].cover.mean():.0%}"` on average.

Across all five cloud models, the largest absolute DR bias is
`{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == DR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['locq'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"` on the
local $+\log\hat q$ map, against
`{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == DR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['loc'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"` on the local
map, `{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == DR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['ols'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"` on the
global OLS map, and
`{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == KR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['locq'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"` for the
local $+\log\hat q$ kriging map alone. A good map limits how much a wrong $\hat q$ can hurt. And
since too little cloud noise costs more than too much, the noise should be calibrated, or erred on
the wide side.

**Not included here.** The covariance is oracle. An Argo-only version would estimate $K$ from the
profiles, which preferential sampling also biases. That affects only the maps, not the validity
argument for the DR step. The window half-width $\lambda$ was fixed at
$`{python} f"{mf.LAM_W:.0f}"`$ km and not tuned.
